claim: Katydids (Insecta) have sophisticated ears, each consisting of paired tympana on each foreleg.
source: Katydids (Insecta) have sophisticated ears, each consisting of paired tympana on each foreleg that receive sound both externally, through the air, and internally via a narrowing ear canal running through the leg from an acoustic spiracle on the thorax.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of katydid ear anatomy.

claim: Katydid ears receive sound both externally through the air and internally via a narrowing ear canal running through the leg from an acoustic spiracle on the thorax.
source: Katydids (Insecta) have sophisticated ears, each consisting of paired tympana on each foreleg that receive sound both externally, through the air, and internally via a narrowing ear canal running through the leg from an acoustic spiracle on the thorax.
evidence: This describes the dual sound input pathways of katydid ears as stated in the abstract.

claim: Katydid ears are pressure-time difference receivers capable of sensitive and accurate directional hearing across a wide frequency range.
source: These ears are pressure-time difference receivers capable of sensitive and accurate directional hearing across a wide frequency range.
evidence: This characterizes the functional properties of katydid ears as stated in the abstract.

claim: Many katydid species have cuticular pinnae which form cavities around the outer tympanal surfaces.
source: Many katydid species have cuticular pinnae which form cavities around the outer tympanal surfaces, but their function is unknown.
evidence: This describes the anatomical feature of pinnae in katydids as stated in the abstract.

claim: The function of cuticular pinnae in katydids was unknown prior to this study.
source: Many katydid species have cuticular pinnae which form cavities around the outer tympanal surfaces, but their function is unknown.
evidence: This states the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The pinnae in C. gorgonensis do not assist in directional hearing for conspecific call frequencies.
source: We found that the pinnae in C. gorgonensis do not assist in directional hearing for conspecific call frequencies, but instead act as ultrasound detectors.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: The pinnae in C. gorgonensis act as ultrasound detectors.
source: We found that the pinnae in C. gorgonensis do not assist in directional hearing for conspecific call frequencies, but instead act as ultrasound detectors.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: Pinnae induced large sound pressure gains (20–30 dB) that enhanced sound detection at high ultrasonic frequencies (>60 kHz).
source: Pinnae induced large sound pressure gains (20–30 dB) that enhanced sound detection at high ultrasonic frequencies (>60 kHz), matching the echolocation range of co-occurring insectivorous gleaning bats.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study stated in the abstract.

claim: The ultrasonic frequency range enhanced by pinnae matches the echolocation range of co-occurring insectivorous gleaning bats.
source: Pinnae induced large sound pressure gains (20–30 dB) that enhanced sound detection at high ultrasonic frequencies (>60 kHz), matching the echolocation range of co-occurring insectivorous gleaning bats.
evidence: This connects the experimental findings to ecological relevance as stated in the abstract.

claim: Katydid pinnae primarily evolved for the enhanced detection of predatory bats.
source: These findings were supported by behavioural and neural audiograms and pinnal cavity resonances from live specimens, and comparisons with the pinnal mechanics of sympatric katydid species, which together suggest that katydid pinnae primarily evolved for the enhanced detection of predatory bats.
evidence: This is the main evolutionary conclusion of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: Early predator detection is a key component of the predator-prey arms race.
source: Early predator detection is a key component of the predator-prey arms race and has driven the evolution of multiple animal hearing systems.
evidence: This is a general statement about evolutionary biology in the introduction.

claim: Early predator detection has driven the evolution of multiple animal hearing systems.
source: Early predator detection is a key component of the predator-prey arms race and has driven the evolution of multiple animal hearing systems.
evidence: This is a general statement about evolutionary biology in the introduction.

claim: Animals with two ears utilize interaural time and amplitude differences to determine the location of a sound source.
source: To determine the location of a sound source, animals with two ears utilize interaural time and amplitude differences.
evidence: This describes a general principle of binaural hearing.

claim: Binaural auditory systems must satisfy three requirements to function: (1) sufficient distance between ears to produce recognizable differences in sound arrival time; (2) ears separated by an anatomical structure large enough to attenuate sound between them; (3) neurological coupling of ears to calculate time and amplitude differences.
source: Such binaural auditory systems must satisfy three requirements to function: (1) the distance between the ears must be sufficient to produce recognisable differences in sound arrival time; (2) the ears must be separated by an anatomical structure which is large enough to attenuate sound between them; (3) the ears must be neurologically coupled in order to calculate time and amplitude differences (Brown, 1984; Christensen-Dalsgaard et al., 2021; Christensen-Dalsgaard and Manley, 2005; Lakes-Harlan and Scherberich, 2015; Lauer et al., 2018; Suga, 1989; Zaslavski, 1999).
evidence: This describes requirements for binaural hearing systems with supporting citations.

claim: Insects are too small to exploit diffractive effects of sound on their bodies to perceive minute differences in sound delays and intensities.
source: However, animals such as insects are too small to exploit diffractive effects of sound on their bodies to perceive minute differences in sound delays and intensities (Michelsen and Larsen, 2008).
evidence: This explains a physical constraint on insect hearing with a supporting citation.

claim: Vastly different species have convergently evolved separate mechanisms of hearing to fulfil similar functions.
source: As a result, vastly different species have convergently evolved separate mechanisms of hearing to fulfil similar functions (Göpfert and Hennig, 2016; Köppl et al., 2014; Robert, 2005; Warren and Nowotny, 2021), including the detection of ultrasonic frequencies (Strauß et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes convergent evolution in hearing systems with supporting citations.

claim: The Tettigoniidae family has over 8100 species.
source: For katydids (or 'bush crickets': Orthoptera: Tettigoniidae), a family with over 8100 species (Cigliano et al., 2021), size may be less of a problem as their ears are located in their two forelegs rather than on their body (Bailey, 1990)
evidence: This provides a taxonomic fact with a supporting citation.

claim: Katydid ears are located in their two forelegs rather than on their body.
source: For katydids (or 'bush crickets': Orthoptera: Tettigoniidae), a family with over 8100 species (Cigliano et al., 2021), size may be less of a problem as their ears are located in their two forelegs rather than on their body (Bailey, 1990)
evidence: This describes the anatomical location of katydid ears with a supporting citation.

claim: The location of katydid ears in their forelegs provides a greater interaural distance and interaural phase difference.
source: For katydids (or 'bush crickets': Orthoptera: Tettigoniidae), a family with over 8100 species (Cigliano et al., 2021), size may be less of a problem as their ears are located in their two forelegs rather than on their body (Bailey, 1990), which provides a greater interaural distance and interaural phase difference, meaning that the resulting distance between the ears provides sufficient spatial separation to exceed the wavelengths of incoming conspecific sounds (Robert, 2005).
evidence: This explains the functional advantage of foreleg ear placement with supporting citations.

claim: Each katydid ear consists of two tympanal membranes on the proximal front tibia (one anterior membrane and one posterior).
source: Each ear consists of two tympanal membranes on the proximal front tibia (one anterior membrane and one posterior), which are both able to receive sound directly at the external tympanal surface (referred as the external input) but also internally through a long, air-filled tube evolutionarily derived from respiratory trachea known as the acoustic trachea or ear canal (ear canal henceforth; Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the anatomical structure of katydid ears with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Sound enters the katydid ear canal through a specialised opening in the prothorax known as the acoustic spiracle.
source: In the internal path, sound enters the ear canal through a specialised opening in the prothorax known as the acoustic spiracle (Kalmring et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes the internal sound pathway with a supporting citation.

claim: The ear canal's narrowing, exponential horn shape passively amplifies sound pressure.
source: The ear canal's narrowing, exponential horn shape passively amplifies sound pressure (Celiker et al., 2020a; Michelsen et al., 1994; Veitch et al., 2021), reduces propagation sound velocity (Jonsson et al., 2016; Michelsen et al., 1994; Veitch et al., 2021), and leads these decelerated sound waves through the thorax and foreleg to the internal tympanal surface.
evidence: This describes the acoustic function of the ear canal with supporting citations.

claim: The ear canal reduces propagation sound velocity.
source: The ear canal's narrowing, exponential horn shape passively amplifies sound pressure (Celiker et al., 2020a; Michelsen et al., 1994; Veitch et al., 2021), reduces propagation sound velocity (Jonsson et al., 2016; Michelsen et al., 1994; Veitch et al., 2021), and leads these decelerated sound waves through the thorax and foreleg to the internal tympanal surface.
evidence: This describes the acoustic function of the ear canal with supporting citations.

claim: The combined phase differences of the internal and external paths generate disparities in sound pressure and arrival times on the external and internal surfaces of the tympanal membranes.
source: The combined phase differences of the internal and external paths generate disparities in sound pressure and arrival times on the external and internal surfaces of the tympanal membranes of each ear.
evidence: This explains how the dual pathways contribute to hearing.

claim: Multiple pathways provide the interaural phase differences to reliably encode the angle of the sound source in katydids.
source: Thus, multiple pathways provide the interaural phase differences to reliably encode the angle of the sound source.
evidence: This explains the mechanism of sound localization in katydids.

claim: The katydid ear functions as a pressure-time difference receiver.
source: The katydid ear therefore functions as a pressure – time difference receiver (Michelsen and Larsen, 2008; Robert, 2005; Veitch et al., 2021), unlike the mammalian ear which functions as a single input pressure receiver via the ear canal.
evidence: This characterizes the functional type of katydid ears with supporting citations.

claim: The mammalian ear functions as a single input pressure receiver via the ear canal.
source: The katydid ear therefore functions as a pressure – time difference receiver (Michelsen and Larsen, 2008; Robert, 2005; Veitch et al., 2021), unlike the mammalian ear which functions as a single input pressure receiver via the ear canal.
evidence: This provides a comparison with mammalian hearing.

claim: Morphologies of cuticular pinnae vary greatly between katydid species.
source: Morphologies of cuticular pinnae vary greatly between species (Figure 1C and D), but their role(s) remain unclear.
evidence: This describes morphological variation with reference to figures.

claim: Before experimental evidence of the dual input system in katydids was published, early observations suggested that pinnae aid in determining the direction of sound.
source: Before experimental evidence of the dual input system in katydids was published (Jonsson et al., 2016; Michelsen et al., 1994), early observations suggested that pinnae aid in determining the direction of sound (Bailey and Stephen, 1978; Autrum, 1963; Autrum, 1942; Autrum, 1940).
evidence: This describes historical hypotheses about pinnal function with citations.

claim: Some researchers suggested that pinnae are merely protective structures sheltering the fragile tympanum.
source: Others suggested that pinnae are merely protective structures sheltering the fragile tympanum (Pumphrey, 1940; Lewis, 1974b).
evidence: This describes an alternative historical hypothesis with citations.

claim: Several authors tested Autrum's hypothesis using electrophysiological techniques and could not demonstrate a role for the pinnae in directional hearing.
source: Subsequently, several authors tested Autrum's hypothesis using electrophysiological techniques and could not demonstrate a role for the pinnae in directional hearing, and instead showed that ear sensitivity depends on sound directed to acoustic spiracles (Lewis, 1974a; Lewis, 1974b; Nocke, 1975; Eisner and Popov, 1978; Hill and Oldfield, 1981; Hoffmann and Jatho, 1995; Michelsen and Nocke, 1974; Shen, 1993).
evidence: This summarizes previous experimental findings with multiple citations.

claim: Lewis (1974b) was the first to suggest a role for the pinnae in maintaining a high sensitivity of the organ at high frequencies.
source: Lewis, 1974b was the first to suggest a role for the pinnae in maintaining a high sensitivity of the organ at high frequencies.

source: Studies of ultrasonic rainforest Pseudophyllinae provided more evidence of principal sound reception for conspecific communication using the external tympanal input instead of their exceptionally small spiracle sizes (Mason et al., 1991).
evidence: This describes findings from a cited study on a specific katydid subfamily.

claim: Diffraction of very short wavelengths along the pinnal cavity entrances produced the strongest responses when stimuli was presented directly opposite the cavity entrances in rainforest katydids.

source: Katydid ancestors (e.g. Haglidae and Prophalangopsidae from Upper Jurassic; Gu et al., 2012; Plotnick and Smith, 2012) and early katydids (Tettigoniidae) from the middle Paleogene (early Eocene; Greenwalt and Rust, 2014; Rust et al., 1999) all show naked tympana without pinnae (likely the plesiomorphic condition).

source: As a working hypothesis, we propose that ear pinnae have a unique origin across the ca. 8,100 living species of Tettigoniidae (Cigliano et al., 2021) in response to the emergence of bats during the early Eocene, and that it was subsequently lost or modified several times.

source: Although katydid ear pinnae have never been mapped in the most recent molecular phylogenies (Song et al., 2020; Mugleston et al., 2018; Mugleston et al., 2013), we observe a potentially unique origin of ear pinnae in the family Tettigoniidae, with multiple losses or retrogressions in modern species, including the large subfamily Phaneropterinae, and the Mecopodinae, predominantly known to have naked tympana.

source: While little is known about the species-specific ecologies and life histories of the Phaneropterinae and Mecopodinae, it would not be surprising that, without pinnal structures, some species evolved sophisticated ear canals with exceptional broadband response for bat detection (Heinrich et al., 1993; Hoffmann and Jatho, 1995; Michelsen et al., 1994; ter Hofstede et al., 2010). This implies that some non-pinnae-bearing species could have a unique ear function via the ear canal, which can detect conspecific calls as well as bats.
